actions.name: Camera inspection of right groin (standing)
actions.result: Visible bulge in right inguinal region, approximately 4 cm, more prominent with standing and Valsalva. Skin intact, no erythema or discoloration. No visible bulge in scrotum.

actions.name: Patient self-reduction maneuver (lying down)
actions.result: Patient reports bulge flattens out completely when lying down and gently pushing; no pain with reduction, mass disappears within a few seconds.

actions.name: Camera inspection for overlying skin changes/discoloration
actions.result: No redness, no dusky or violet discoloration, no skin breakdown over the bulge.

actions.name: Video-observed reduction maneuver
actions.result: On camera, patient demonstrates reducing the bulge himself: gentle manual pressure while supine causes the mass to flatten completely within seconds; no grimacing or guarding observed during the maneuver, consistent with an easily, painlessly reducible hernia.

actions.name: Review home vital signs (BP cuff, pulse ox)
actions.result: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 78 bpm regular, temp 98.2°F, SpO2 97% on room air.

actions.name: Review home weight/BMI documentation
actions.result: Height 5'10" (178 cm), weight 216 lb (98 kg), BMI 31 kg/m2, consistent with prior visits.

actions.name: Review groin ultrasound report
actions.result: Right inguinal hernia, indirect type, containing omental fat, fully reducible, no bowel loop identified, no evidence of strangulation.

actions.name: Review current medication list
actions.result: Aspirin 81 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, no anticoagulants, no other prescription medications listed.

actions.name: Review recent CBC and basic metabolic panel
actions.result: Hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL (13.5-17.5), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400), sodium 139 mmol/L (136-145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (0.7-1.3) - all within normal limits.

actions.name: Review HbA1c
actions.result: HbA1c 5.7% (<5.7% normal, 5.7-6.4% prediabetes) - borderline, no prior diagnosis of diabetes.

actions.name: Review smoking history/pack-year documentation
actions.result: Current smoker, 1 pack per day x 30 years (30 pack-years), has not attempted quitting per prior visit notes.

actions.name: International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) administered
actions.result: IPSS total score 16/35 (moderate symptom range), driven by weak stream, straining, and incomplete emptying domains; no hematuria or fever reported on associated screening questions.

actions.name: Review prior post-void residual/urology note if available
actions.result: No urology referral or post-void residual study on file; tamsulosin was prescribed by primary care for symptomatic benign prostatic enlargement 18 months ago, no further workup documented.

actions.name: Operative risk stratification (ASA class / functional capacity)
actions.result: ASA class II (uncontrolled/untreated hypertension, obesity, tobacco use); reports walking long distances at truck stops and climbing into cab daily without chest pain or dyspnea, consistent with greater than 4 METs functional capacity.

artifacts.title: Groin Ultrasound Report
artifacts.author: Radiology, Outpatient Imaging Center
artifacts.body:
CLINICAL HISTORY: Right groin bulge, intermittent discomfort.

FINDINGS: There is a right inguinal hernia with a defect identified lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, consistent with an indirect inguinal hernia. The hernia sac contains omental fat. On provocative (Valsalva) maneuver, the hernia protrudes and reduces spontaneously and with gentle manual pressure. No bowel loop is identified within the sac. Doppler flow within adjacent structures is normal. No free fluid. No evidence of incarceration or strangulation.

IMPRESSION: Reducible right indirect inguinal hernia containing omental fat, no bowel involvement, no sonographic signs of incarceration.

artifacts.title: Primary Care Visit Note - Tobacco Use
artifacts.author: Dr. R. Alvarez, Primary Care
artifacts.body: Mr. Petrov continues to smoke approximately 1 pack per day, started around age 20, for an estimated 30 pack-year history. Counseled on cessation including nicotine replacement and prescription options; patient states he is not ready to quit at this time due to stress of long-haul driving schedule. Will readdress at future visits.

artifacts.title: Primary Care Visit Note - Urinary Symptoms
artifacts.author: Dr. R. Alvarez, Primary Care
artifacts.body: Patient reports progressive urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and straining over several months. Digital rectal exam deferred by patient preference at that visit. Started tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily for presumed benign prostatic enlargement. Advised follow-up with urology if symptoms worsen or fail to improve; no urology referral placed to date per chart review.

objectives.text: Elicit a hernia history that confirms indication for elective repair (chronicity, reducibility, absence of incarceration red flags) despite patient minimization of symptoms

Identify and counsel on modifiable perioperative risk factors: smoking, obesity, aspirin management, and undiagnosed lower urinary tract symptoms that could precipitate postoperative urinary retention
Explain open versus laparoscopic/mesh repair options and address patient concerns about mesh safety using accurate, non-dismissive language
Counsel on realistic return-to-driving and lifting timelines appropriate to occupational demands, balancing patient's work pressure against safe recovery
Recognize incarceration/strangulation warning signs to teach the patient for self-monitoring during the preoperative waiting period

Identify the aspirin/perioperative medication mismatch between patient's plan and appropriate guidance, and recognize the undiagnosed BPH/urinary retention risk that may warrant primary care or urology input before or around surgery

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states the bulge and discomfort are 'not a big deal' and he can 'live with it'
mismatches.recordEvidence: Patient-reported size trend chart shows the bulge nearly tripling in estimated size over 12 months (1.5 cm to 4 cm)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients, especially those motivated to avoid time off work, may understate symptom severity; eliciting a careful functional and chronologic history (effect on driving tolerance, timing of aching) reveals a more significant clinical picture than the patient's framing suggests, and objective size trend data corroborates this progression.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient plans to simply stop his aspirin 'a day or two before' surgery on his own
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list shows aspirin 81 mg daily listed for cardiovascular prophylaxis with no documented history of MI, stroke, or peripheral arterial disease, and no structured perioperative plan on file; the correct approach (continue vs. stop, and for how long) depends on clarifying with the prescribing clinician whether this is primary or secondary prevention, not on the patient unilaterally picking a stop date
mismatches.teachingPoint: Perioperative medication management, especially antiplatelet agents, must follow an explicit documented plan coordinated with the prescribing clinician rather than patient-initiated discontinuation, to avoid both excess bleeding and (if there is a true atherosclerotic indication) thrombotic risk; the indication for aspirin (primary vs. secondary prevention) should be clarified first since this changes the risk-benefit calculus and determines whether stopping or continuing is actually preferred.

scenario.studentBrief: You are a general surgery resident conducting a telehealth pre-operative consultation with Viktor Petrov, a 59-year-old truck driver referred for evaluation of an enlarging, aching right groin bulge. He is requesting elective repair during his upcoming 3-week work layoff. Your job is to assess his symptoms, confirm the surgical indication, assess his operative risk, discuss repair options and risks, and address his questions about timing.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Enlarging, aching right groin bulge for about a year, patient requesting elective repair during his upcoming 3-week work layoff
scenario.openingLine: I've got this lump in my right groin that's been there about a year. It's bigger now. I want it fixed during my three weeks off next month.
tasks: Take a focused history of the presenting concern and review any available imaging
Assess perioperative risk factors including relevant medical history, medications, and social history
Explain surgical repair options and address the patient's questions and concerns
Counsel on realistic timelines for return to driving and lifting given his occupation
Teach warning signs to watch for in the preoperative period and discuss perioperative medication management

answerKey.primaryProblem: Symptomatic, reducible right indirect inguinal hernia confirmed by ultrasound, appropriate for elective surgical repair
differential: Direct inguinal hernia (less likely given ultrasound description of indirect defect lateral to inferior epigastric vessels)
Femoral hernia (not supported by exam/imaging location)
Hydrocele or varicocele (ruled out by absence of scrotal/testicular findings)
Lipoma of groin (ruled out by ultrasound showing true hernia defect)
keyFindings: One-year history of progressively enlarging right groin bulge with end-of-day aching, now ultrasound-confirmed indirect inguinal hernia containing fat
Hernia always fully reducible, no history of incarceration, no overlying skin changes, no nausea/vomiting - no current emergent features
30 pack-year current smoker, not yet ready to quit
BMI 31, untreated/lifestyle-managed hypertension (BP 138/86 today), ASA class II

On aspirin 81 mg daily apparently for primary cardiovascular risk reduction (no documented history of MI, stroke, or peripheral arterial disease) without a documented perioperative plan; patient intends to self-stop it a day or two before surgery on his own rather than through a coordinated plan

Undiagnosed, undertreated urinary symptoms (weak stream, straining, nocturia; IPSS 16/35 moderate) on tamsulosin for 18 months without urology follow-up - a recognized risk factor for postoperative urinary retention
Patient significantly minimizes symptom severity relative to the history of progressive enlargement and worsening aching
plan: Confirm elective operative indication; schedule repair within the patient's 3-week layoff window if medically feasible, favoring open or laparoscopic mesh repair based on shared decision-making

Discuss open vs. laparoscopic (TEP/TAPP) mesh repair approaches, including recovery differences, and provide balanced, evidence-based counseling on mesh safety to address his lawsuit-advertisement concerns, correcting misconceptions without dismissing them

Review and address modifiable risk factors: strongly recommend smoking cessation (even short-term preoperative abstinence reduces wound and pulmonary complication risk) and offer referral to cessation resources

Clarify with the prescribing clinician whether aspirin is for primary or secondary cardiovascular prevention, since this determines the correct perioperative approach: for primary prevention without documented atherosclerotic disease (the likely scenario here), perioperative discontinuation coordinated with the prescribing clinician is often reasonable because the bleeding-risk reduction outweighs the marginal cardiovascular benefit, and the ongoing need for aspirin itself should be revisited with primary care; for secondary prevention with documented atherosclerotic disease, continuation through this low-bleeding-risk hernia repair is generally favored. In either case, any change must follow an explicit documented plan rather than the patient stopping it on his own a day or two beforehand

Refer to primary care or urology for proper evaluation of lower urinary tract symptoms (consider post-void residual, possible BPH workup) before surgery, given risk of postoperative urinary retention, which is outside general surgery's scope to independently diagnose or manage definitively

Provide explicit counseling on realistic return-to-driving (commercial driving typically restricted at least 1-2 weeks after mesh repair, pending surgeon clearance and any DOT medical requirements) and lifting restrictions (typically no heavy lifting over approximately 10-15 lbs for about 2 weeks, with gradual return) tailored to his job duties

Teach incarceration/strangulation warning signs: sudden inability to reduce the hernia, severe or worsening pain, nausea/vomiting, fever, or skin discoloration over the bulge - instruct to seek emergency care immediately if these occur before scheduled surgery
Obtain informed consent documenting discussion of recurrence risk, chronic groin pain, urinary retention, and other standard risks/benefits/alternatives
redFlags: Sudden inability to reduce the hernia (possible incarceration)
Severe or rapidly worsening groin pain
Overlying skin erythema, warmth, or discoloration (possible strangulation)
Acute urinary retention (inability to void) - requires urgent evaluation, outside elective timeline
educationPoints: A reducible, asymptomatic-seeming hernia can still be clinically significant; a careful chronologic and functional history (not just a device-generated trend) is the primary tool for uncovering progression in patients who minimize symptoms

Hernia mesh is generally safe and is the evidence-based standard of care for most inguinal hernia repairs; publicized lawsuits often relate to specific product recalls or other mesh types (e.g., transvaginal mesh) rather than inguinal hernia mesh broadly, and this distinction should be explained clearly and respectfully

Whether low-dose aspirin should be continued or stopped before a low-bleeding-risk procedure like hernia repair depends on the indication: for primary prevention without documented atherosclerotic disease, perioperative discontinuation (coordinated with the prescribing clinician, never self-directed) is often appropriate because bleeding-risk reduction outweighs the marginal cardiovascular benefit, and the ongoing need for aspirin itself should be revisited with primary care; continuation is favored when aspirin is for secondary prevention of documented atherosclerotic disease. In no case should the patient decide on his own to stop it a day or two before surgery

Preoperative smoking cessation, even for a short period before surgery, meaningfully reduces wound healing and pulmonary complication risk and should be addressed at every opportunity without being punitive

Undiagnosed or undertreated benign prostatic symptoms raise the risk of postoperative urinary retention after hernia repair under anesthesia, and should prompt referral for proper urologic evaluation rather than being overlooked because the surgical complaint is unrelated
Occupational return-to-work counseling (driving, lifting) should be concrete and individualized, balancing the patient's economic pressures against safe tissue healing timelines

profile.title: Pre-operative consultation for symptomatic right inguinal hernia in a 59-year-old truck driver
profile.summary: A 59-year-old male truck driver with a one-year history of enlarging, symptomatic right indirect inguinal hernia seeks surgical repair during his three-week winter layoff. The case teaches pre-operative risk assessment (smoking, obesity, urinary symptoms), informed consent for mesh herniorrhaphy, patient education about realistic recovery timelines for physically demanding work, and recognition of modifiable perioperative risks including smoking cessation and undiagnosed benign prostatic hyperplasia.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient calling from a motel-style room between trucking routes
